processing: Gongfu black tea from one bud and two leaves, shaped into long, straight, tight strands.
harvest_season: One bud and two leaves. A higher tin-packed version uses one bud with one or two leaves from high, cold areas.
appearance_dry: Tight, straight, long dark strands with a little golden down.
appearance_liquor: Typically a clear red, as with other Fengqing Dian Hong.
appearance_wet: Typically coppery whole leaf and bud, as with other Dian Hong at this picking standard.
taste_profile: Sweet potato and honey on the nose, fairly full and reasonably fresh in the mouth, with some flower-and-honey sweetness.

brewing.notes: Sturdy and forgiving. It also suits an everyday mug at about 3 g per 250 ml for 2 to 3 minutes.

vintage_note: A continuously made product rather than a vintage tea, sold in kraft bags and tins of 200 g to 380 g. Check the production date and drink it within a year or two. Same-name packs can differ in leaf tenderness, so read which version you are buying.
description:
Classic 58 is the everyday black tea of Fengqing, sold under the Feng brand and among the best-known names in Dian Hong. It is a house recipe rather than a type of tea, but it comes up so often that it is worth knowing, and many drinkers meet Dian Hong through it.

It is picked at one bud and two leaves, a modest standard compared with the all-gold teas, then shaped into long, straight strands with only a little gold showing. That leaves more leaf body and less bud sweetness.

In the cup it smells of honey and sweet potato and drinks full and fairly fresh. It is not delicate, which makes it a good daily tea that tolerates a heavy hand.

The packaging matters: the kraft bag and square tin hold the same leaf, while the round tin uses more tender high-altitude material and costs more. Compare it with Fengqing's Song Zhen or gold-bud teas to taste what picking standard does.
history: The 58 is often assumed to refer to 1958, but no source checked here confirms that, and the origin of the name and recipe is not documented. The tea comes from the Feng brand of the former Fengqing tea factory, which goes back to the Shunning experimental factory of 1939, where Dian Hong's early production took shape.
